Yet, the optimization of SKU-to-pod assignment remains a critical challenge, especially when considering realworld operational constraints such as SKU variability and physical storage limitations. This research proposes a structured, data -driven SKU allocation policy aimed at optimizing pod space utilization while improving throughput and pile-on performance in RMFS environments.

The methodology integrates demand frequency, product turnover, item correlation, and dimensional feasibility into a unified classification and placement strategy. SKUs are first categorized by demand frequency using K-means clustering, and further classified based on demand stability using the Coefficient of Variation.

These classifications are applied under three allocation configurations: Random placement, One Pod One Class, and One Pod Mixed Class. To further enhance accessibility, a dispersion policy is introduced to distribute SKUs across multiple pods . A simulation model developed in NetLogo, combined with optimization modules in Python, evaluates performance under dimensional constraints and with the dispersion policy applied.

Results in dicate that under dimensional constraints, the One Pod Mixed Class strategy achieved the highest performance, with throughput reaching 91.90% and pile-on 9.79, followed by One Pod One Class and the Random baseline. The introduction of the dispersion policy further improved both metrics across all scenarios, with throughput increasing to 99.22% and pile -on to 9.96 for Mixed Class . Statistical validation using ANOVA confirmed significant differences in throughput and pile -on among the three scenarios under both dimensional constraints and with the dispersion policy. Paired t-tests further verified that dispersion produced statistically significant improvements in both metrics for all s cenarios. These results demonstrate that combining demand -based classification with dispersion and dimensional feasibility leads to more effective SKU - to-pod assignments in RMFS environments. Keywords: Robotic Mobile Fulfillment System, SKU Allocation, Storage Assignment, Coefficient of Variation, Dimensional Constraints, Mixture, Dispersion, Order Throughput, Pile-On. iii ACKNOWLEDGEMENT First and foremost, I would like to express my deepest gratitude to my principal advisor, Professor Shou -Yan Chou, for his invaluable guidance, encouragement, and support through out the course of my research and thesis writing. 45 1 CHAPTER 1 INTRODUCTION 1.1 Background and Motivation The e -commerce sector has witnessed exponential growth in recent years, significantly reshaping global retail operations and consumer purchasing behaviors. As of 2024, the global logistics market for e-commerce is estimated at approximately USD 500.76 billion, with projections estimating a rapid increase to USD 609.59 billion in 2025, and exceeding USD 3.7 trillion by 2034, reflecting a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 22.3% [1].

This surge of expansion is primarily driven by the rising demand for fast, accurate, and technology-supported logistics services, especially in the B2C segment. The evolution of this market is illustrated in Figure 1.1, which shows the projected regional growth of e -commerce logistics from 202 0 to 2034, highlighting the dominant role of North America and the fast -growing influence of Asia Pacific. Figure 1. 1 E-Commerce Logistics Market Size by Region [1] In addition to major e -commerce players like Amazon, a growing number of department stores and supermarkets have also provided online shopping platforms. This widespread shift has significantly expanded the scale of distribution centers and delivery operations [2].

This rapid rise of e-commerce has been significantly accelerated by the COVID - 19 pandemic, which acted as a major catalyst for digital transformation in the retail sector. Widespread lockdowns and social distancing policies compelled many bric k 2 and mortar retailers to temporarily shut down physical stores, prompting an urgent shift toward digital commerce and technology-driven fulfillment solutions.

This shift led to the rapid adoption of systems such as online ordering, click-and-collect services, and robotics -assisted operations to maintain continuity in order fulfillment under restrictive conditions [3], [4]. Prior to the pandemic, traditional e-commerce fulfillment relied heavily on manual labor for handling and processing orders [5]. However, as demand surged and efficiency requirements grew more stringent, many warehouses began transitioning toward automation [6]. Recent advancements in robotics have enabled the emergence of hybrid fulfillment models that combine human labor with autonomous agents, improving accuracy, scalability, and responsiveness [7], [8].

This transition toward automation has fundamentally transformed the logistics and warehousing landscape, but it has also introduced new operational challenges. Modern e-commerce warehouses must now cope with a large assortment of SKUs, frequent small-batch orders, strict delivery windows, and highly variable workloads throughout the day [9]. One of the most labor-intensive and costly operations within a warehouse is order fulfillment, particularly the order picking process , the retrieval of items to complete customer orders which accounts for 55% of the total warehouse operating expenses [10], [11], [12] . Moreover, o nly about 40% of direct labor activities are devoted to productive tasks like loading, unloading, stocking, and picking, whereas the remaining 60% is primarily spent on unproductive travel within the warehouse [13]. Due to these rising complexities of e -commerce orders, traditional manual picking systems struggle to maintain efficiency. As a result, many warehouses have started integrating automation technologies, such as Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems, to optimize operations. Wurman et al.

[14] introduced a pioneering approach to warehouse automation, proposing the use of autonomous mobile robots to transport storage units, later termed “pods”, to designated locations known as “workstations,” where human operators complete the picking process. This innovative system, which became widely known as the Kiva system, laid the foundation for a new generation of robotic fulfillment solutions [15], [16]. Since its initial deployment by Kiva systems in 2012 [17], the Robotic Mobile Fulf illment System has gained widespread adoption in global e - commerce warehouses. Leading companies such as Amazon, Walgreens, Staples, 3 JD.com, and Alibaba’s Cainiao Network have integrated RMFS into their order fulfillment operations to enhance efficiency and scalability [18]. Figure 1. 2 Shelves in Amazon Warehouse [19] Figure 1. 3 Workflow in RMFS Warehouse [20] The components within RMFS are highly interdependent, creating a complex operational environment. While the system offers massive improvements over traditional warehousing methods, it also introduces a range of decision -making problems.

Research on RMFS ha s predominantly focused on addressing various optimization, assignment, and scheduling problems to enhance overall system performance [21]. While the optimization of RMFS has been extensively investigated by scholars in recent years, research on categorized storage remains limited.

Current studies primarily focus on improving robot routing, order sequencing, and pod retrieval 4 strategies, yet t he fundamental problem of efficient SKU allocation to storage locations has not received the same level of attention. In RMFS warehouses, the way SKUs are assigned to pods significantly impacts retrieval efficiency, system throughput, and overall warehouse performance [2]. A poorly optimized SKU allocation strategy may lead to excessive pod retrievals , higher energy consumption and longer order fulfillment time. Another critical issue in SKU-to-pod assignment is pile-on efficiency, which refers to the number of items that can be picked from a single pod visit. In an optimized RMFS, frequently co -ordered SKUs should be stored together in the same pod to reduce the number of pod retrievals per order [22]. Poor SKU placement disrupts this balance, forcing robots to retrieve multiple pods for a single order. Consequently, retrieval delays increase, fulfillment speeds decline, and warehouse throughput is negatively affected.

In light of these challenges, this research specifically investigates the issue of SKU allocation in RMFS warehouses, aiming to assign SKUs to pods in a way that maximizes order throughput and pile -on. By leveraging historical order data , specifically SKU order frequency , order quantity and dimensional constraints, this study seeks to develop a storage assignment optimization model that enhances picking efficiency and operational performance. 1.2 Objective The primary objective of this research is to develop an effective SKU allocation strategy for Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems (RMFS) t hat enhances storage efficiency and order fulfillment performance. Specifically, this study aims to: 1. Increase order throughput by designing a SKU-to-pod assignment approach that reduces pod retrieval delays and supports continuous picking operations. 2. Improve pile-on efficiency by grouping frequently co-ordered SKUs within the same pod to maximize the number of items that can be picked from a single pod visit. 3.

chunks.text: 1.3 Scope and Limitations This study is conducted within a defined scope and under specific assumptions, described as follows: • The primary focus in this study is on small order sizes with multi-item orders typical of e-commerce fulfillment. Large bulk orders are excluded from this study and are assumed to be handled at separate warehouse facilities. • This study focuses exclusively on the SKU-to-pod assignment policy within warehouse operations. Other key processes, such as order -to-station assignment (POA – Pick Order Assignment) and pod -to-station assignment (PPS – Pick Pod Selection), dynamic replenishment, and robot routing are handled using brute-force methods rather than optimized algorithms. • The data used for simulation is ad apted from actual cases, with the study modeling a total of 7,024 unique SKUs to reflect a realistically large SKU range. • All SKUs, including those with low demand, are assumed to be stored in the warehouse. Each pod is designed with multiple compartments, and each compartment can contain only a single type of SKU. • The Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs) modeled in this study are assumed to perform both picking and replenishment tasks . However, the assignment of of AMRs to specialized task are beyond the scope of this work. Additionally, this study does not address the battery charging or management aspects of AMR operations. • It is assumed that the replenishment station always maintains adequate inventory levels to meet replenishment demand, ensuring that SKUs are always available when required during pod replenishment process. • The warehouse environment is modeled using an Agent -Based Modeling (ABM) approach implemented in NetLogo. The simulation integrates Python 6 for optimization tasks and u ses Excel for data management and storage of simulation results.

chunks.text: 7 CHAPTER 2 LITERATURE REVIEW 2.1 Robotic Mobile Fulfillment System (RMFS) Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems have emerged as a transformative innovation in warehouse logistics, particularly within the e-commerce sector. Unlike traditional picker-to-parts systems where workers walk through aisles to retrieve items [23], RMFS follows a parts-to-picker approach, where autonomous mobile robots transport storage units called pods, directly to human -operated or automated picking stations [20]. Several studies have shown that incorporating RMFS into warehouse systems can significantly cut down picker travel time, making higher picking rates more doable compared to traditional warehouse setups [24]. Today, RMFS is widely adopted by leading companies such as Alibaba, JD.com, and Cainiao, significantly improving warehouse productivity and cost efficiency [25], [26], [27]. In RMFS, the core components include: 1.

chunks.text: Pods: Movable shelves that store various Stock Keeping Units [28]. Each pod consists of multiple compartments designed to hold items of different sizes and categories. A single pod may carry several types of products, depending on the SKU -to-pod assignment strategy adopted. When a pick or replenishment order is generated, the system identifies the appropriate pod(s) containing the required SKUs and instructs a robot to fetch them. 2.

chunks.text: Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs): battery-powered robots that are capable of navigating warehouse environments using a grid of waypoints and pre - defined paths [29]. Each robot is equipped with a lifting mechanism that allows it to move underneath a pod, lift it, and carry it to the designated workstation [30]. Once the task is completed, the robot returns the pod to an optimized storage location based on inventory rules. Advanced RMFS platforms use intelligent robot scheduling and path planning algorithms to avoid congestion, prevent deadlocks, and minimize travel distances. 8 Figure 2. 1AMRs and Pods [31] 3.

At a picking station, workers retrieve items from the pod to fulfill customer orders. For replenishment, the robot delivers a pod to a replenishment station where new inventory is added to maintain stock levels. chunks.text: At this stage, one of the key considerations is workstation placement, which involves deciding where to p osition picking and replenishment stations in relation to the storage area. Another important factor is storage area dimensioning, which includes determining the overall size of the storage space, how it’s divided into zones, and how aisles are arranged. 10 Tactical decisions in an RMFS are typically made at the beginning of an operational period, such as the start of a workweek, workday or shift. These decisions involve determining number of pods per SKU, ratio of pick and replenishment stations, replenishment level, and resource reallocation.

Operational-level decisions are executed in real time and directly govern the flow of robots, pods, and orders. These are the most dynamic and data-driven decisions in an RMFS and are divided into four main components: 1. chunks.section: 4. Path Planning (PP) deciding where to place a pod after it completes a task,
chunks.text: When products with high correlation are placed together within the same pod, they are more likely to be appeared together in a single order [41]. This increases the number of items that can be retrieved in a single pod trip, thereby reducing the overall number of pod visits required to complete order fulfillment. By understanding how products are frequently ordered together, researchers and practitioners can identify meaningful relationships that helps clustering, scattered storage policies, and mixed storage configurations. This data-driven perspective helps RMFS warehouses boost picking efficiency, reduce unnecessary robot travel, and adapt dynamically to changing demand patterns.

chunks.text: Market Basket Analysis is one of the most widely applied techniques for uncovering these item relationships that associated with customer buying behaviour [42]. MBA relies on Association Rule Mining to analyze transaction data, detecting which items appear together in customer orders. Furthermore, a dispersion policy was introduced to inves tigate the effect of distributing SKUs across multiple pods, thereby increasing SKU accessibility. A simulation model was developed using NetLogo for agent -based modeling and Python for optimization, and performance was evaluated using a dataset of 7,024 SKUs. Simulation results showed that under dimensional constraints alone, the One Pod Mixed Class strategy achieved the best performance, with mean throughput of 91.90% and mean pile‑on of 9.79, followed by One Pod One Class with mean throughput of 85.23% and mean pile‑on of 9.37 and the Random baseline with mean 53 throughput of 78.65% and mean pile‑on of 7.35. The current classification framework is primarily based on demand stability . However, additional factors such as SKU physical size, weight, and handling complexity could be integrated into the classification criteria to create more comprehensive storage profiles.
